hits.name: Corey Ganim
hits.text:
Claude shipped Whiteboard, Sheets, Data, and Meetings in 3 days. My raw thoughts:

1) This is the Microsoft Office period for AI. Office bundled Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, basically killing Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect.

2) Notetakers are going to feel the most pressure. Notes, action items, and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise during the beta. Hard to charge per seat for that now.

3) Something I find very interesting: Anthropic is "partnering" with Granola, Fireflies, Otter, and Gong. Claude records the meeting and they become where the transcript gets sent.

4) Gong is safe (for now). Claude stays out of any call with an outside guest by default (i.e. sales calls)

5) Doing real work inside a call is the product here. Being able to say "Claude, start a doc for this plan" that your team can edit mid-call is a real efficiency gain.

6) Interactive connectors are one of the recent updates nobody is talking about. Adobe, Atlassian, and Box now open INSIDE Claude. It seems that Anthropic knows which tools it can't replace. They're choosing to host those instead.

7) The pattern is clear, they're coming for just about everything. Docs, boards, sheets, dashboards, meetings, and your bank balances (Personal Finance shipped Nov 5). Who knows what's next?

8) I think vertical SaaS is Anthropic's next play. Claude for Legal got a contract review gallery last month while Claude for Manufacturing launched today with 17 skills for quotes and quality reports.

9) Meetings ships inside Google Meet only and on Team and Enterprise only (for now, in beta). If you're a HIPAA or zero-data-retention org, you shouldn't touch it yet. Zoom shops and healthcare will have to wait.

10) Perfect time for your org to audit your stack and figure out which tools you're currently paying for that are now bundled in with your Claude subscription.

11) Even with all these new features, Anthropic has done a great job in keeping the Claude app SIMPLE. This is where OpenAI has really dropped the ball. The ChatGPT app is incredibly complex and confusing by contrast.

Such an incredible time to be a builder and on the forefront of AI. Remember, most of humanity still has zero grasp of these tools!

hits.draft_en:
Four Claude launches in 3 days - Whiteboard, Sheets, Data and Meetings. How I read it:

- AI just reached its Microsoft Office moment. Bundling Word, Excel and PowerPoint is what finished off Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect.
- Notetaker apps get squeezed first. During the beta, Team and Enterprise get transcripts, notes and action items at no cost, so per-seat pricing becomes a tough sell.
- The twist: Granola, Fireflies, Otter and Gong are now "partners". Claude does the recording, and those tools are where transcripts end up.
- Gong looks fine for the moment, since by default Claude skips calls that include an outside guest, like sales calls.
- The actual product is getting work done mid-call. Ask Claude to start a doc for the plan and the whole team edits it while still talking.
- Underrated: interactive connectors. Adobe, Atlassian and Box now open within Claude - Anthropic hosts the tools it knows it can't replace.
- Direction is obvious: docs, boards, sheets, dashboards, meetings, even your bank balances, with Personal Finance out since Nov 5.
- Vertical SaaS looks like the next move. Claude for Legal picked up a contract review gallery last month, and Claude for Manufacturing arrived with 17 skills covering quotes and quality reporting.
- Caveats: Meetings is Google Meet only, Team and Enterprise only, still beta. HIPAA and zero-data-retention orgs should hold off; Zoom shops and healthcare wait.
- Good moment to audit which paid tools your Claude subscription already covers.
- Despite all of it, the Claude app stays simple. OpenAI missed that - next to it the ChatGPT app feels complex and confusing.

Great time to build. Most people still have no idea what these tools can do.

hits.name: Thorsten Ball
hits.text:
What's the right team size?

Probably not the one you set in 2024.

Think about it: your infrastructure team was 8 people back then, but now, with each person able to do so much more, faster, is 8 still the right size?

Do you have more infrastructure to manage? If you have more infrastructure, then maybe. If not, you no longer need 8 people on that team.

If the the ambitions of the company align with the increased productivity of teams, that's great, of course. But not every team in every company needs to scale up. 

If your business success isn't a function of how much infrastructure you manage (to keep using that example), then you want to keep the amount of work the infra team does fixed. And that amount requires less people now.

Product teams, on the other hand, can now do a lot more and very likely should. But there the question is: does the org allow that?

I was talking to @lewis_b_metcalf yesterday about some engineers really crashing out and lamenting the loss of craft.

He said: "Yeah, I get it. If you're in a company where all you were hired for and all you're allowed to do is engineering, then things might suck. But here [at Amp], I can do marketing, I can think of new product ideas, I can ship them, talk to users, record videos. I can do so much more and it's the most fun I ever had."

That's, I think, the crux of the matter: your engineers won't become 10x more effective if your org doesn't allow them to.

If you haven't done this four times this year already, it's high time to rethink all of your org boundaries and roles.

Of course AI won't have an impact on your business if your engineers are sitting there, twiddling their thumbs, waiting for someone to hand them a ticket.

hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Every AI company I've talked to is solving the same problem:

How to let several agents write to the same data without one silently undoing another's work?

Omnigraph is an open-source graph database that versions data the way developers already version code:

↳ Each agent writes on its own branch
↳ Omnigraph checks every merge against the latest main
↳ A policy blocks direct writes to main

GitHub repo: https://t.co/WBovu3DeOi

(don't forget to star it 🌟)

To test this, I gave Codex and Claude Code one shared graph of services and teams, with one task each, as shown in the video below:

- Codex moved a service from RabbitMQ to Kafka.
- Claude Code handed that same service's on-call to a new engineer.

Both agents started from the same version of that service.

Codex merged cleanly, but Claude Code got flagged for a conflict, rebuilt its change on the latest main, and then merged.

A row lock only helps when two agents hit the same record at the same moment.

But an agent's task usually touches many records over several minutes. A branch keeps that whole change isolated until it merges, and each merge leaves a diff you can review and a history of who changed what.

Omnigraph is written in Rust, and agents connect to it over MCP.

I shared the GitHub repo above.

To dive deeper, I wrote a full breakdown of why shared agent data needs branches, diffs, and merge checks, not just row locks.

It walks through a real run with two Claude Code agents, from the refused merge to the clean retry. Read it below.

Read it below.

hits.name: may.crypto {🦅}
hits.text:
become a market maker on Polymarket. one bot like this makes ~$800 a day, 19 months straight.
  
i broke down how to build one:

tl;dr: it makes money on the spread. it buys from people who want out and sells to people who want in

its markets are crypto price levels: will BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP hit $X this week/month/year. in options this is called a one-touch.

on every level it keeps two limit orders: a buy a bit below the price and a sell a bit above.

risk/reward of this setup

reward - the spread. bought NO at 91¢, sold it 11 hours later at 95¢. that's about two thirds of its money. on top of that Polymarket pays makers rebates and liquidity rewards, another
  ~10%

risk - shares it bought and didn't sell in time. they stay with it until the market closes, and if the price hits the level the wrong way, they go to zero

in january it lost $44k on those shares. reselling made $74k the same month, and january closed +$30k

MVP step by step:

1 - pull the market list from Polymarket's Gamma API: the "what price will bitcoin hit" events, same for ETH, SOL, XRP. every level there is its own market with its own order book

2 - place orders through the official py-clob-client. the bot reads the level's book and keeps two limit orders: a buy a bit below the mid, a sell a bit above

3 - subscribe to the websocket for your own fills. the moment a buy fills, the bot posts a sell above the buy price

4 - in parallel the bot watches BTC on Binance. when it gets close to a level, pull your orders on that level. otherwise your limit gets taken at the old price before you can cancel it

5 - keep size small on every level. unsold leftovers are your risk

here's the profile of a bot like this: https://t.co/cCaq39grM8

As a screenwriter, I struggle to get real feedback on a script. My friends in film are busy and tired of reading their 1000th draft, and paid coverage is expensive. So I built a Screenplay Review Panel that runs on my laptop.

It's an open-source agent skill I built with Claude Code and Antigravity. It runs seven specialist readers on your own machine, each as its own subagent: dialogue, description, formatting, character, structure, an audience reader and a festival programmer. They read your draft in parallel, debate it, and hand you ranked line edits that you approve one at a time. In the tutorial I run it with Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

Here's the full 10-minute tutorial: how to install it and run it on your own screenplay.

I made the animated intro and outro with Gemini Omni (video), Gemini TTS (the narrator's voice) and Lyria (music), and directed the whole edit from Antigravity. The tutorial is a real screen recording. I only sped up the agents' waiting time.

outsiders.text:
As a screenwriter, I struggle to get real feedback on a script. My friends in film are busy and tired of reading their 1000th draft, and paid coverage is expensive. So I built a Screenplay Review Panel that runs on my laptop.

It's an open-source agent skill I built with Claude Code and Antigravity. It runs seven specialist readers on your own machine, each as its own subagent: dialogue, description, formatting, character, structure, an audience reader and a festival programmer. They read your draft in parallel, debate it, and hand you ranked line edits that you approve one at a time. In the tutorial I run it with Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

Here's the full 10-minute tutorial: how to install it and run it on your own screenplay.

I made the animated intro and outro with Gemini Omni (video), Gemini TTS (the narrator's voice) and Lyria (music), and directed the whole edit from Antigravity. The tutorial is a real screen recording. I only sped up the agents' waiting time.
